findings.title: In-process cache makes an authorization decision incoherent across replicas
findings.description: api/permissions.py:8 caches allow/deny in a module-level dict with a 300s TTL. The service runs multiple replicas, so each process holds an independent view of a security decision: after a revocation, whether a request is allowed depends on which replica serves it, for up to five minutes. This inverts the fail-closed property an authorization check must have — the cache preserves a stale allow rather than falling back to a deny. The premise of caching this particular lookup in-process is not repairable by tuning the TTL.
findings.suggested_action: Do not cache the decision in-process. If lookup latency is the motivation, cache in a shared store with explicit invalidation on permission change, or cache the inputs rather than the decision.

findings.title: Cache is unbounded
findings.description: api/permissions.py:5 — _PERM_CACHE has no size limit and no eviction beyond the TTL check on read. Entries for (user_id, resource_id) pairs that are never read again are retained for the process lifetime, so memory grows with the cardinality of that pair space.
findings.suggested_action: If a cache survives review at all, bound it and evict on write, not only on read.

new_questions.question: What measured latency problem motivated caching this lookup? The answer determines whether a shared-store cache is even needed.
new_questions.why: The motivation for the change is not recorded in the repository; only the author knows what was measured.
